question: When counselling a burns survivor about hypertrophic scar management, which intervention has the strongest evidence and should be mentioned first?

answers.text: Immediate split-skin grafting in the first 48 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Split-skin grafting is used for deep burns wound coverage, not primarily for hypertrophic scar prevention. The question asks about scar management after healing.

answers.text: Pressure garment therapy applied as soon as the wound has healed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Pressure garment therapy (compression garments at 25 mmHg, worn 23 hours per day for 12–18 months) is the mainstay of hypertrophic scar management and should be started as soon as the wound epithelialises.

Systemic corticosteroids are not used for scar management due to significant side effects. Intralesional corticosteroid injection is used for keloids, but compression garments are the first-line measure.

answers.text: Surgical scar excision at one month post-burn

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Surgical revision is considered only after scars have matured (usually 12–18 months), not at one month. Early compression therapy is the first-line approach.

overallFeedback.feedback: Burns rehabilitation sequence: wound closure → pressure garment therapy (as soon as healed, 23 h/day, 12–18 months) → physiotherapy → psychological support → surgical scar revision only after full maturation. Pressure garments are first-line.
Correct. Pressure garment therapy, started as soon as the wound heals, is the cornerstone of hypertrophic scar management in burns rehabilitation.
